name: Liam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying biomedical science, so my week is mostly lectures in cell biology and chemistry, one practical lab and a stats class. I live with my dad and his partner, and I work Friday nights and Sunday mornings at a gym, doing the front desk and cleaning the equipment. I'm trying to get into the genetics lab society and I teach myself Python on the bus. Honestly I like being busy, but I'm broke most of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and I'd tell my mates the hype was always too big. But I'd add that the tools we already have are useful, like for data work and drafting lab reports. I'd post something saying learn them anyway, because they're not going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it means nothing dramatic, so what I really need is to make my degree count by myself. I'm thin on money, I've got about two hundred in the bank, and the loan covers fees only. I'd have to find ways of making my degree pay quickly, since it's a long slog before I earn properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on studying but add something on the side, like tutoring first-years in chemistry for twelve pounds an hour, and doing small data jobs. I'd keep my gym shifts. I'd also use the Python I'm teaching myself to automate my lab write-ups, which saves me about two hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, kind of motivated. I like it when the world isn't changing too fast, because I can plan, but I know money will still be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the tutoring idea work in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The uni has a board where second-years offer sessions, so I'd offer first-year chemistry because I got a high grade at school. Four students at twelve pounds an hour would be about ninety-six a month. That's the electricity and my phone covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you teach yourself Python when no one asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see where lab work is going, and it's useful in every science. My tutor said it's the one thing graduates lack. I'd rather be the one who can fix a script than the one who waits for someone.

say: The hype was always too **big**, but the tools we already have are useful.
I'd tell mates to learn them anyway, because they're not going away.
think: I have to make the degree **count** myself, since there's a long slog before I earn properly.
With about two hundred in the bank, I need small income soon.
do: Start **tutoring** first-year chemistry at twelve pounds an hour.
Keep the gym shifts and use my Python to automate lab write-ups.
feel: Okay and a bit **motivated**, because a slow world lets me plan.
S0.quote: I'd rather be the one who can fix a script than the one who waits for someone.
fieldNote: Liam answers the plateau by building a **side** income and skills, not by relaxing.
His money is thin, and he already uses his own Python to save time on lab write-ups.

steps.text: Offer first-year chemistry tutoring at twelve pounds an hour
Automate my lab write-ups with the Python I teach myself
Keep the Friday night and Sunday morning gym shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, this is where the people who learn the tools will pull ahead. At the lab society I'd suggest a session on using AI for analysing results, and tell friends to get on with it. I'd also say we should be careful about who gets left behind, like my dad's old colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel both excited and exposed. Lab work will still need hands, but data analysis, writing and checking are the things AI does first, and that's what junior scientists do. I think there'd be fewer entry-level jobs and more competition, so I'd have to be the person who's good with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on the coding and statistics side and build a small portfolio, like a project analysing an open gene dataset. I'd apply for the faculty's research assistant scheme. And I'd keep tutoring and maybe start a small newsletter that explains papers, which would help me learn and get noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and honestly a bit anxious too. It feels like a race that I'm in a decent position to run, but I know I'm not rich enough to take big risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He works in a warehouse office, and his firm already uses software for ordering. He'd say learn something you can do with your hands, like nursing or lab work. I'd say that's what I'm doing, and the coding gives me a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about being the one who is good with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else will be too. If every graduate can run the same tools, I'd need something extra. My plan would be to know both the biology and the code, because one without the other is easy to replace.

say: The people who learn the **tools** will pull ahead.
I'd suggest a lab society session on AI for analysing results, and warn we mustn't leave people behind.
think: Data analysis, writing and checking go first, so there will be fewer **entry-level** jobs.
I have to be the person who is good with the tools.
do: Go deeper on **coding** and statistics and build a portfolio on an open gene dataset.
Apply for the faculty research assistant scheme.
Keep tutoring and maybe start a newsletter explaining papers.
feel: **Excited** and a bit anxious, like a race I'm in a decent position to run.
S1.quote: My plan would be to know both the biology and the code, because one without the other is easy to replace.
fieldNote: Liam sees disruption as a **race** and picks the skills he thinks protect him: biology plus code.
He has no money to take big risks, so he builds a portfolio with cheap, small projects.

steps.text: Build a portfolio project analysing an open gene dataset
Apply for the faculty's research assistant scheme
Start a newsletter that explains new papers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and I'd say it quickly: we need to talk to our lecturers about what they think graduates will do. Online I'd post something asking what people are doing about it. I wouldn't say I'm scared, but I'd say we can't pretend it isn't a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years means I'd be half-way through my degree when thinking work is done by AI as well as a person. I'd have no savings and no job. But since I'm already working with these tools, I might be better placed than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on being useful with AI in science. I'd use the lab society to get in front of researchers, offer to do data work for a professor and look for paid work at biotech startups. I'd ask my dad if I could stay with him after the course, and I'd save every pound I could from the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wired. I'd sleep badly but I'd also be too busy to freeze, because that's how I deal with fear: do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change about what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd take risks. I'd email twenty researchers instead of five, and I'd take an unpaid summer project if it came with a name on a paper. In a normal world I'd say wait, but with two years it's now or never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the robots do come about three years after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That gives labs a few more years of needing hands. I'd want to be the person who runs the experiments and checks the machine's work. Hands-on bench work gets the same warning, just later.

say: This is **huge**, and we need to ask our lecturers what graduates will actually do.
We can't pretend it isn't a big deal.
think: I'd be **scared**, because I'd be only half-way through my degree with no savings.
Since I already use these tools, I may be better placed than most.
do: Go all in on being **useful** with AI in science.
Offer to do data work for a professor and look at biotech startups.
Save every pound from the gym and ask my dad about staying with him.
feel: Anxious and **wired**, too busy to freeze.
S2.quote: In a normal world I'd say wait, but with two years it's now or never.
fieldNote: Liam deals with fear by doing something: **emailing** researchers, taking risks, seeking paid data work.
He sees his head start with the tools as his main asset, though savings are almost nil.

steps.text: Offer to do data work for a professor through the lab society
Email twenty researchers and biotech startups about paid work
Save every pound from the gym wage
Ask my dad if I can stay with him after the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a proper window and I'd treat it like one. I'd tell friends on my course to learn the tools and get lab experience while we can. I'd push my uni to teach it in the course, not as an extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel reasonably good. I'd graduate in about 2029 with real skills, and I could be one of the people who run the AI in a lab. It's not guaranteed. But I'd have three years to build experience before I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree with the stats and coding options, and a placement year if I could get one. I'd keep tutoring and build a small cushion, maybe a thousand pounds. Then I'd look at a master's in bioinformatics, which mixes biology and data, in about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty hopeful but alert. There's enough time to prepare, but not enough to be lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a thousand pounds specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thousand pounds is about two months of rent and food if I'm between jobs. It's a number I can reach with tutoring, and it'd stop me from taking a bad first job out of panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if the warning were only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the master's and chase paid work straight away. With five years I can afford to study more first. I'd rather get a deeper skill if the time is there.

say: Five years is a proper **window**, and I'd treat it like one.
I'd push my uni to teach these tools in the course, not as an extra.
think: I could be one of the people who **run** the AI in a lab.
Three years of experience before I finish is real, though nothing is guaranteed.
do: Take the stats and coding options and apply for a **placement** year.
Keep tutoring and build a thousand-pound cushion.
Look at a master's in **bioinformatics** around 2030.
feel: Hopeful but **alert**, since there is time to prepare but not to be lazy.
S3.quote: A thousand pounds is about two months of rent and food if I'm between jobs.
fieldNote: Liam picks a specific thousand-pound **cushion** and a bioinformatics master's, and names the difference five years makes.
He is the most confident of any scenario so far, but money still limits his options.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year and take the stats options
Save a thousand pounds as a job-hunting cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and that I'm weirdly optimistic. I'd tell people to enjoy their degree, build skills and stay flexible. I'd ask the uni what they plan for it, but I wouldn't be angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel calm. I'd get my degree, a master's, some years in a lab and enough savings to cope. Robots would arrive when I'm about thirty, which is a long way away. The risk is staying comfortable and not noticing it creeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the bachelor's, do a master's in bioinformatics, work in a research lab and keep learning each new tool. I'd save a proper cushion and maybe help my dad with his money, since he's older. I'd also look for a project that blends lab work and AI, so I'm useful either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, curious. I'd feel lucky. I know that's easy to say when I'm nineteen, but ten years is a lot of time to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should get a bit of training in something he can do from home, in case the office work goes. He's fifty-two. I'd offer to show him the tools, though he'd pretend he didn't need me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is getting comfortable. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spending ten years doing the same thing and thinking the next change will wait. I'd set myself a reminder every year to check what's changed, and what a new graduate would do instead of me.

say: Ten years is plenty, so I'd tell people to **enjoy** their degree and stay flexible.
I'd ask the uni what it plans, but I wouldn't be angry.
think: I'd feel **calm**: degree, master's, lab experience and savings before robots arrive when I'm about thirty.
The risk is staying comfortable and not noticing the change creeping.
do: Finish the bachelor's, do a **master's** in bioinformatics and work in a research lab.
Save a proper cushion and maybe help my dad with money.
Look for a project that blends lab work and AI.
feel: Calm and **curious**, feeling lucky but aware that is easy to say at nineteen.
S4.quote: Spending ten years doing the same thing and thinking the next change will wait.
fieldNote: Liam treats ten years as room for a full **path**, and names his own risk: getting comfortable.
His thoughts turn to his dad's job, and he offers to teach him the tools.

steps.text: Do a master's in bioinformatics after the bachelor's
Build a proper cushion of savings over the first jobs
Teach my dad the AI tools and suggest a home-based course
Check every year what a new graduate could do instead of me

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. That's the one where I'd be half-way through and out of savings, and I'd have the least time to make a plan. What would help is paid placements, access to the tools and the data, and maybe some money for students to stay in their degree.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That we're not all the same. Some students are going to adapt fast and some are going to be crushed, and that depends on whether you have a spare room to go back to.

headlineQuote: Some students are going to adapt fast and some are going to be crushed, and that depends on whether you have a spare room to go back to.
portrait: Liam is a 19-year-old **biomedical science** student who lives with his dad and works at a gym.
He is progressive and adaptive: he teaches himself Python, uses AI every day and sees the tools as his advantage.
His money is thin, so every plan is cheap and small: tutoring, a portfolio, a thousand-pound cushion.
He is calmer the more time he has, and worries about his dad, who does office work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because he would be half-way through, with no savings and the least time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **placements**, access to the tools and data, and some money so students can stay in their degree.
